lines.text: In 1914, the US mail delivered a parcel that giggled.
Her name was May, she was five years old,
and the stamps to ship her cost fifty-three cents.
They went right on her little coat.
She went seventy-three miles through the post,
and the rule that allowed it?
Well, there wasn't one.
The post office patched that loophole by summer anyway.
And for fifty years, nobody dared mail a whole human being again.
Until a champion read the rulebook a little... differently.
Two people went through the mail on purpose. Both stories true.
Let's rewind back to May.
In 1914, May's family lived on a farm near Grangeville, Idaho,
and grandma's place was in Lewiston, seventy-three miles of hills away.
And May wanted to visit her. Badly.
But the train ticket cost three times more
than what the postage would run her.
So her dad walked up to the post office counter
and asked the most dangerous question in US history:
So... what does it cost to mail a little kid?
Because 1913 had just invented parcel post, and trains took packages now.
The clerk flipped through the big rulebook, sweating.
The rulebook covered bees, it covered baby chicks, it went on and on...
But nothing in there said no.
So May climbed up onto the scale,
forty-eight and a half pounds,
just one pound and a half under the fifty pound parcel limit.
She was legal.
Then on went fifty-three cents of stamps on her coat,
and her mom's cousin Leonard took the handoff,
because he just happened to be the railway mail clerk.
May rode the next train, right in the mail car,
sitting on the mail sacks, waving at whatever trains wave at.
When the train pulled in, Leonard walked her up the hill
and delivered her to grandma's front door.
Grandma got the parcel. May got seventy-three miles of adventure.
But Washington did not laugh.
The newspapers told the whole country about the girl in the mail,
and that summer, the Postmaster General made it official:
no person may ever be sent through the mail.
You could still mail day-old baby chicks, though.
The rulebook got a new page, and May went back to normal mail. For fifty years.
Until... London, 1964.
The star of part two: a broke Australian
and his five foot wooden box.
Reg Spiers. Two metres of champion javelin thrower from Adelaide.
He'd already thrown for Australia at the Commonwealth Games in Perth.
Now he was chasing a spot at the Tokyo Olympics
when an injury blew the whole plan up.
So Reg took an airport job in the cargo shed,
saving every pound for the flight home to his wife
and his little daughter, whose birthday was creeping up.
And then one London morning, his wallet vanished.
Every saved pound inside it. Gone.
So: no ticket, and a birthday countdown already running.
Now, Reg had spent months watching animals go through that shed
as ordinary air freight,
and one idea crawled into his head:
If they can do it, I can do it.
He knew the rulebook too. The maximum crate gate:
five by three by two and a half feet.
Two metres of champion, folded into five feet of box.
His friend John built one in a London workshop
big enough to sit with straight legs, or lie
with your knees bent.
Both ends were loose panels held by wooden pegs.
Pegs that Reg could knock out FROM THE INSIDE.
And on the label? A load of paint.
Headed to an Australian shoe company that did not exist.
And the genius bit: he shipped himself cash on delivery.
London pays nothing today. Whoever catches the parcel
all the way over in Perth, pays for it later.
Loaded in with him: tinned food, a torch, a blanket,
a pillow, and two plastic bottles.
One was for water.
I'll let you guess about bottle number two.
London fog held the flight a full extra day,
so Reg's first twenty-four hours were pure lying-in-a-box patience.
A grown man lying in the dark, being very, very patient.
Then, airborne. And when the plane finally levelled out,
Reg knocked the pegs out and climbed out to stretch his legs.
Then the plane began to sink toward Paris,
so back in the crate he went, leaving his you-know-what can on top.
The French handlers found that can, blamed the English,
and said some terrible things about the English.
Down in the hold, nobody had noticed. He was still just a crate of paint.
Next stop, Bombay. Where ground crews parked his crate
upside down, in the sun, for four straight hours.
The quote: "Sweating like a pig, but not giving up."
Then came the sound: Australian accents swearing about heavy crates.
And that noise means Perth. That noise means home.
Three days. Sixty-three hours. In one wooden box.
The crate rolled straight into a locked customs shed.
Reg knocked the pegs out, found a crate of beer,
and toasted his freedom with a free beer. He doesn't even drink.
Then, tools sitting right there, he cut a hole in the wall,
put on his suit, because flying barely creases a suit,
and jumped through the window to hitch a ride into town.
Meanwhile, worried John had called the newspapers from London,
so when Reg got home, the press was already there,
and camped on his street for weeks.
The airline never sent him one single bill.
And a politician wired five quid: "a gallant effort by a real Aussie."
The birthday? He made it. Presents, delivered.
His wife did not believe a word of it at first.
Then she did the math: how else would you get here?
And that 1914 rule, no people in the mail?
Reg Spiers read it as more of... a suggestion.
May: five years old, fifty-three cents, seventy-three miles.
Reg: twenty-two, 63 hours in a crate, half a planet.
The post office never planned to be a passenger airline.
It was just... really bad at saying no.
